---
title: "Dates, Times & Durations"
subtitle: "≈ lubridate · hms"
jupyter: python3
---

Polars has four temporal dtypes and one namespace, `.dt` (parsing lives in
`.str`). This chapter follows R4DS 2e's *Dates and times* on `flights`: build
a datetime from parts, take it apart, round it, measure spans, and move it
between time zones. How a `Datetime` is stored (µs since the epoch, zone in
the dtype) is in [Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-physical); the
one-line lubridate translations are in the
[cheatsheet](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-datetime).

## In tidyverse {#sec-dt-tidyverse}

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(nycflights13)

make_datetime_100 <- function(year, month, day, time) {
  make_datetime(year, month, day, time %/% 100, time %% 100)
}

flights_dt <- flights |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_time), !is.na(arr_time)) |>
  mutate(across(c(dep_time, arr_time, sched_dep_time, sched_arr_time),
                \(t) make_datetime_100(year, month, day, t))) |>
  select(origin, dest, ends_with("delay"), ends_with("time"))

flights_dt |> count(wday = wday(dep_time, label = TRUE))   # components
flights_dt |> count(week = floor_date(dep_time, "week"))   # rounding

one_am <- ymd_hms("2013-03-10 01:00:00", tz = "America/New_York")
one_am + ddays(1)   # duration: 2013-03-11 02:00:00 EDT
one_am + days(1)    # period:   2013-03-11 01:00:00 EDT

with_tz(flights$time_hour[1], "Asia/Bangkok")              # time zones
```

R has three classes for a point in time (`Date`, `POSIXct`, `hms::hms`), and
lubridate adds three for a span: **duration** (exact seconds), **period**
(clock units such as days and months) and **interval** (a span anchored at a
start). `make_datetime()` defaults to `tz = "UTC"`, so R4DS's `flights_dt`
holds New York clock times labelled UTC. Polars has four dtypes, expresses
periods as strings passed to a method, and has no interval type.

## Mental model {#sec-dt-model}

```text
 dtype            ≈ R                  stored as (to_physical)         .dt.* reads it as
 ───────────────  ───────────────────  ──────────────────────────────  ──────────────────────────
 Date             Date                 Int32  days since 1970-01-01    a calendar day
 Datetime(u, tz)  POSIXct + tzone      Int64  u since 1970-01-01 UTC   the wall clock in tz
 Time             hms::hms             Int64  ns since midnight        a clock time, no day
 Duration(u)      duration, difftime   Int64  u                        elapsed time; no months

 one instant, two labels                        two ways to move it
 ─────────────────────────────────────────      ───────────────────────────────────────────────
 1357034400000000 µs ─┬─► America/New_York       fixed     + pl.duration(days=1), "24h"
                      │   2013-01-01 05:00 EST             adds exact µs          ≈ ddays(1)
                      └─► Asia/Bangkok           calendar  .dt.offset_by("1d"), "1mo"
                          2013-01-01 17:00 +07             moves the wall clock   ≈ days(1), months(1)

 convert_time_zone(): same µs, new label   ≈ with_tz()
 replace_time_zone(): same label, new µs   ≈ force_tz()
```

## Mechanics {#sec-dt-mechanics}

```{python}
#| include: false
%xmode Minimal
```

```{python}
import datetime as dt

import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs
from pl_notes import datasets

flights_df = datasets.flights()
weather_df = datasets.weather()
```

### Build a datetime from parts {#sec-dt-build}

`pl.datetime()` is `make_datetime()`: it takes literals or columns, and `//`
and `%` split the HHMM integers:

```{python}
#| error: true
dep = pl.col("dep_time")
flights_df.select(pl.datetime("year", "month", "day", dep // 100, dep % 100))
```

`dep_time` writes midnight as `2400` (29 flights; 150 for `arr_time`), and
`pl.datetime()` rejects hour 24. Build midnight of the day, then add the clock
time as a `Duration`; hour 24 rolls over to the next day:

```{python}
def make_datetime_100(time: str) -> pl.Expr:
    """year/month/day columns + an HHMM integer column → naive Datetime."""
    hhmm = pl.col(time)
    midnight = pl.datetime("year", "month", "day")
    return (midnight + pl.duration(hours=hhmm // 100, minutes=hhmm % 100)).alias(time)

flights_df_dt = (
    flights_df.filter(pl.col("dep_time").is_not_null(), pl.col("arr_time").is_not_null())
    .with_columns(
        make_datetime_100(c) for c in ["dep_time", "arr_time", "sched_dep_time", "sched_arr_time"]
    )
    .select("origin", "dest", cs.ends_with("delay"), cs.ends_with("time"))
)
flights_df_dt.head(3)
```

`.alias(time)` is required: an expression is named after its leftmost input,
which is `year` for all four
([naming rules](../core/expressions.qmd#sec-expr-naming)). The result is
**naive**: clock times with no zone, which is what R4DS's "UTC" label really
meant. @sec-dt-tz attaches the zone.

### Time units {#sec-dt-units}

A `Datetime` or `Duration` counts in one unit, fixed by the dtype: `"us"`
(the default), `"ns"` (which only reaches 1677–2262 in an Int64) or `"ms"`.
When two units meet, Polars converts both to the **coarser** one and silently
drops the finer digits:

```{python}
units_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"t_ns": pl.Series([1_357_032_600_000_000_123]).cast(pl.Datetime("ns"))}
).with_columns(t_ms=pl.col("t_ns").cast(pl.Datetime("ms")))

units_df.with_columns(
    same=pl.col("t_ns") == pl.col("t_ms"),          # compared in ms → true
    plus_1h=pl.col("t_ns") + pl.duration(hours=1),  # µs duration → µs result
    offset_1h=pl.col("t_ns").dt.offset_by("1h"),    # keeps ns
)
```

Set the unit explicitly with `.dt.cast_time_unit()` or
`pl.duration(..., time_unit="ns")`; `.dt.with_time_unit()` was removed in
2.0. `pl.concat()` refuses mixed units unless `how="vertical_relaxed"`, which
again picks the coarser one.

### Parsing strings {#sec-dt-parse}

`str.to_date()`, `str.to_datetime()` and `str.to_time()` take a chrono format
(mostly R's `strptime` codes; `%.f` is fractional seconds);
`str.strptime(dtype, format)` is the same with the dtype as an argument. With
a format, parsing is exact and strict:

```{python}
#| error: true
pl.Series(["2013-01-31", "2013-02-30"]).str.to_date("%Y-%m-%d")
```

`strict=False` turns the failures into null (lubridate's "failed to parse",
without the warning).

Without a format, Polars tries a short list of patterns, takes the first one
that parses a value, and applies that **one** pattern to the whole column, so
`["2013-01-01", "01/02/2013"]` fails on the second value. Slash dates are
read day first, and month first is not on the list:

```{python}
pl.Series(["01/02/2013", "15/02/2013"]).str.to_date().to_list()   # 1 Feb, not 2 Jan
```

```{python}
#| error: true
pl.Series(["12/31/2013"]).str.to_date()      # month first: no pattern fits
```

Inference is fine for clean ISO strings. Otherwise pass the format, the same
choice as `ymd()` vs `dmy()` vs `mdy()`.

An offset (`%z`, or a trailing `Z` when inferring) produces a UTC column: each
value is shifted to UTC and the offset is dropped; `time_zone=` then sets the
display zone. On strings *without* an offset, `time_zone=` attaches the zone
to the clock time instead, like `ymd_hms(x, tz = ...)`:

```{python}
stamps_df = pl.DataFrame({"raw": ["2013-01-01T05:17:00+07:00", "2013-01-01T05:17:00-05:00"]})
fmt = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z"

stamps_df.with_columns(
    utc=pl.col("raw").str.to_datetime(fmt),
    bkk=pl.col("raw").str.to_datetime(fmt, time_zone="Asia/Bangkok"),
    local_ny=pl.col("raw").str.slice(0, 19).str.to_datetime(time_zone="America/New_York"),
)
```

Also: `time_unit="ns"` keeps nanosecond digits (the default `"us"` truncates
them), and `exact=False` finds a date inside a longer string.

### Components {#sec-dt-components}

```{python}
dep = pl.col("dep_time")
flights_df_dt.select(
    "dep_time",
    year=dep.dt.year(),
    month=dep.dt.month(),
    yday=dep.dt.ordinal_day(),
    wday=dep.dt.weekday(),
    hour=dep.dt.hour(),
    month_name=dep.dt.strftime("%B"),
    wday_abbr=dep.dt.strftime("%a"),
    clock=dep.dt.time(),
).head(3)
```

- `weekday()` runs Monday = 1 … Sunday = 7, which is
  `wday(x, week_start = 1)`; lubridate's default is Sunday = 1.
- Components are small integers: `Int8` for month, day, hour, minute,
  weekday, week and quarter, `Int16` for `ordinal_day()`, `Int32` for
  `year()`. Arithmetic on them can overflow (@sec-dt-int8).
- Names come from `strftime()`, in English. Where `wday(label = TRUE)` gives an
  ordered factor, sort by the number and carry the name as a label.
- `.dt.time()` returns a `Time` (≈ `hms::as_hms()`), `.dt.date()` a `Date`.
- `week()` is the ISO week (≈ `isoweek()`): 2012-12-31 is week 1 of ISO year
  2013, so pair it with `iso_year()`. lubridate's `week()` is
  `(ordinal_day() - 1) // 7 + 1`.
- `.dt.replace(year=2030, hour=9)` is `update()`. lubridate rolls an
  out-of-range value over (`mday = 30` in February becomes 2 March);
  `replace()` raises "Invalid date components".

### Rounding {#sec-dt-rounding}

`truncate()` is `floor_date()`, `round()` is `round_date()`, and both take an
interval string:

```{python}
moments_df = pl.DataFrame({"t": [dt.datetime(2013, 1, 31, 5, 17, 40), dt.datetime(2013, 2, 14, 17, 45, 10)]})
t = pl.col("t")

moments_df.with_columns(
    floor_15m=t.dt.truncate("15m"),
    round_1h=t.dt.round("1h"),
    floor_week=t.dt.truncate("1w"),
    floor_month=t.dt.truncate("1mo"),
    month_start=t.dt.month_start(),
)
```

- **Weeks start on Monday**; `floor_date(x, "week")` starts on Sunday. For
  Sunday weeks, shift, truncate, shift back:
  `t.dt.offset_by("1d").dt.truncate("1w").dt.offset_by("-1d")`.
- `month_start()` and `month_end()` move the *day* and keep the clock time,
  so on a `Datetime` they are not `truncate("1mo")`.
- There is no `ceiling_date()`: `truncate(every)` then `offset_by(every)`,
  leaving values that already sit on a boundary alone.

### Offsets: calendar vs fixed {#sec-dt-offset}

`offset_by()` is period arithmetic. An interval string is a count and a unit;
units chain (`"1h30m"`, `"1mo1d"`) and negate (`"-1q"`):

```text
 fixed (exact elapsed time)            calendar (moves the wall clock)
 ns  us  ms  s  m  h                   d  w  mo  q  y
             ▲                         ▲      ▲
          MINUTE                     DAY    MONTH       "1m" is a minute; a month is "1mo"
```

In a naive column the two families agree, since a naive day is always 24 h.
They split when the zone has DST. New York sprang forward on 2013-03-10:

```{python}
dst_df = pl.select(t=pl.datetime(2013, 3, 9, 9, time_zone="America/New_York"))
t = pl.col("t")

dst_df.with_columns(
    offset_1d=t.dt.offset_by("1d"),        # calendar: same clock time  ≈ days(1)
    offset_24h=t.dt.offset_by("24h"),      # fixed: 24 h later          ≈ ddays(1)
    plus_days_1=t + pl.duration(days=1),   # a Duration's days are fixed too
).with_columns(elapsed_1d=pl.col("offset_1d") - t)
```

`pl.duration(days=1)` and `dt.timedelta(days=1)` are 24 hours: duration
arithmetic. Only `offset_by()`, `truncate()`, `round()` and the range
functions understand calendar units.

Months differ in length. `offset_by("1mo")` clips to the last valid day, like
`%m+%` (plain `+ months(1)` gives `NA` for 31 January):

```{python}
month_ends_df = pl.DataFrame({"d": [dt.date(2013, 1, 31), dt.date(2012, 2, 29)]})
d = pl.col("d")

month_ends_df.with_columns(
    plus_1mo=d.dt.offset_by("1mo"),
    plus_1mo_twice=d.dt.offset_by("1mo").dt.offset_by("1mo"),   # clipping sticks
    plus_2mo=d.dt.offset_by("2mo"),
    plus_1y=d.dt.offset_by("1y"),
    minus_1q=d.dt.offset_by("-1q"),
)
```

`by=` also takes an expression, so the offset can vary per row:
`d.dt.offset_by(pl.format("{}mo", pl.col("n_months")))`.

### Durations {#sec-dt-durations}

Subtracting two datetimes (or two dates) gives a `Duration`. Scheduled and
actual departures are both New York clock times:

```{python}
flights_df_dt.filter(pl.col("dep_delay") > 60).select(
    "sched_dep_time", "dep_time",
    late=pl.col("dep_time") - pl.col("sched_dep_time"),
).with_columns(
    minutes=pl.col("late").dt.total_minutes(),
    hours=pl.col("late").dt.total_hours(),                       # truncates toward 0
    hours_frac=pl.col("late").dt.total_hours(fractional=True),
    hours_div=pl.col("late") / pl.duration(hours=1),            # ≈ late / dhours(1)
).head(3)
```

The third flight did not leave 9 hours early. It left at 08:48 the *next*
day (`dep_delay` is 853), but `make_datetime_100()` gave it the scheduled
date (the overnight recipe has the fix). It also shows `total_*()` returning
an `Int64` truncated toward zero: −9.78 hours becomes −9.

| lubridate / base R | Polars |
|---|---|
| `d2 - d1` (a `difftime`, auto units) | `d2 - d1` (a `Duration`, shown as `1h 41m`) |
| `as.numeric(x, units = "hours")`, `x / dhours(1)` | `.dt.total_hours(fractional=True)`, `x / pl.duration(hours=1)` |
| duration: `ddays(1)`, `x + dminutes(n)` | `pl.duration(days=1)`, `x + pl.duration(minutes=pl.col("n"))` |
| `dyears(1)` (365.25 days), `dmonths(1)` | none: `pl.duration()` stops at `weeks=` |
| period: `x + days(1)`, `x %m+% months(1)` | `x.dt.offset_by("1d")`, `x.dt.offset_by("1mo")`: a string, not a dtype |
| interval: `x %within% (a %--% b)` | no dtype: keep `a` and `b` as columns, `x.is_between(a, b)` |

: lubridate's three spans {.striped}

A `Duration` can be summed, averaged, and multiplied or divided by a number.

### Time zones {#sec-dt-tz}

`flights.time_hour` is stored in UTC and labelled `America/New_York` (see
`datasets.py`). Converting changes the label, not the stored number;
replacing keeps the clock time and changes the number:

```{python}
zones_df = flights_df.select(
    "time_hour",
    bkk=pl.col("time_hour").dt.convert_time_zone("Asia/Bangkok"),     # with_tz
    forced=pl.col("time_hour").dt.replace_time_zone("Asia/Bangkok"),  # force_tz
).head(1)
zones_df
```

```{python}
zones_df.select(pl.all().to_physical())   # time_hour and bkk: the same instant
```

`.dt` methods read the **local** clock: `hour()` is 5 on `time_hour` and 17
on `bkk`, and `truncate("1d")` cuts at local midnight.

`replace_time_zone()` is also how a naive column gets its zone:
`flights_df_dt["dep_time"].dt.replace_time_zone("America/New_York")` attaches
New York, and `convert_time_zone()` can follow. `replace_time_zone(None)`
drops the zone and keeps the clock time; `convert_time_zone()` on a naive
column assumes UTC. Zones are IANA names;
an abbreviation such as `"ICT"` raises, and `"+07:00"` becomes the fixed zone
`Etc/GMT-7`.

#### DST edges: `ambiguous=` and `non_existent=` {#sec-dt-dst}

A clock time can map to two instants or to none. When New York fell back on
2013-11-03, 01:00 happened twice, and `weather` records both:

```{python}
jfk_df = weather_df.filter(
    pl.col("origin") == "JFK",
    pl.col("time_hour").dt.date() == dt.date(2013, 11, 3),
    pl.col("hour") <= 2,
).select("year", "month", "day", "hour", "time_hour")
jfk_df
```

Rebuilding `time_hour` from the clock columns with
`pl.datetime(..., time_zone="America/New_York")` raises "datetime
'2013-11-03 01:00:00' is ambiguous". `ambiguous=` takes `"raise"` (default), `"earliest"`, `"latest"` or `"null"`,
or an expression giving one of those per row. One choice for all rows can't
recover both readings; a per-row choice can:

```{python}
first_one = pl.col("hour").is_first_distinct()   # the first 01:00 is the earlier
ny_clock = {"time_zone": "America/New_York"}

jfk_df.select(
    "time_hour",
    earliest=pl.datetime("year", "month", "day", "hour", **ny_clock, ambiguous="earliest"),
    per_row=pl.datetime(
        "year", "month", "day", "hour", **ny_clock,
        ambiguous=pl.when(first_one).then(pl.lit("earliest")).otherwise(pl.lit("latest")),
    ),
)
```

The lesson is R's too: when DST is in play, store instants, not clock parts.
The other edge is spring forward: 02:30 on 2013-03-10 never happened in New
York, so `replace_time_zone()` raises "non-existent"; `non_existent=` takes
only `"raise"` (default) or `"null"`. Bangkok has never observed DST, so a Bangkok clock time is never ambiguous.

### Ranges and grouping by period {#sec-dt-ranges}

`pl.date_range()` and `pl.datetime_range()` are `seq()` for dates. They return
an expression unless `eager=True`:

```{python}
pl.date_range(dt.date(2013, 1, 31), dt.date(2013, 5, 31), "1mo", eager=True).to_list()
```

Each element is `start + k months`, so the range returns to the 31st after
February, unlike the chained `offset_by()` above. A zoned `datetime_range()`
follows the local clock (hourly steps on 2013-03-10 skip 02:00), and
`date_range()` accepts whole days only (`"1h"` raises).

Grouping by a period is grouping by a truncated value
(`group_by(month = floor_date(time_hour, "month"))`). On a zoned column the
groups start at local midnight:

```{python}
weather_df.filter(pl.col("origin") == "JFK").group_by(
    month=pl.col("time_hour").dt.truncate("1mo")
).agg(
    temp=pl.col("temp").mean().round(1),
    n_hours=pl.len(),
).sort("month").head(4)
```

`group_by_dynamic()` (overlapping or offset calendar windows) and `rolling()`
belong to a later time-series chapter; time-based `rolling_*_by()` is in
[Window Functions](../transform/window.qmd).

## Where it bites {#sec-dt-gotchas}

| lubridate / R | Polars |
|---|---|
| `"1 month"`, `months(1)` | `"1mo"`; `"1m"` is a **minute** (@sec-dt-1m) |
| `wday()`: Sunday = 1; weeks start Sunday | `weekday()`: Monday = 1 … Sunday = 7; `truncate("1w")` gives Mondays |
| POSIXct in different zones compare as instants | different zones, or aware vs naive: `SchemaError` (@sec-dt-compare) |
| `x < "2013-01-02"` coerces the string | comparing with a string raises |
| `Date + hours(5)` becomes a date-time | `Date + Duration` stays `Date`; hours are dropped (@sec-dt-date-plus) |
| `hour(x) * 60` can't overflow | `Int8` arithmetic wraps (@sec-dt-int8) |
| `update(x, mday = 30)` rolls over into March | `dt.replace()` raises; so does `pl.datetime()` on hour 24 |
| `ymd()` / `dmy()` / `mdy()`: you name the order | no format: one inferred pattern per column, slashes day-first (@sec-dt-parse) |
| `%y`: 69 → 1969 | `%y`: 69 → 2069 (00–69 → 20xx) |
| one numeric type for times | mixed time units fall to the coarser unit (@sec-dt-units) |

: The differences at a glance {.striped}

### `"1m"` is a minute {#sec-dt-1m}

On a `Datetime`, the typo gives the wrong grain with no error:

```{python}
flights_df.select(
    groups_1m=pl.col("time_hour").dt.truncate("1m").n_unique(),
    groups_1mo=pl.col("time_hour").dt.truncate("1mo").n_unique(),
)
```

On a `Date`, `offset_by()`, `truncate()` and `round()` with any sub-day
interval do nothing, again silently. Only `date_range()` refuses one.

```{python}
pl.DataFrame({"d": [dt.date(2013, 1, 31)]}).with_columns(
    offset_1m=pl.col("d").dt.offset_by("1m"),
    offset_1mo=pl.col("d").dt.offset_by("1mo"),
)
```

### Zones must match, except for a `date` {#sec-dt-compare}

A naive literal against a zoned column raises, and so does a literal in UTC
or any other zone:

```{python}
#| error: true
flights_df.filter(pl.col("time_hour") < dt.datetime(2013, 1, 1, 6))
```

A `datetime.date` literal does **not** raise. It is cast to midnight UTC,
which is 19:00 the previous evening in New York, so the filter quietly drops
flights. Build the literal in the column's zone, or compare dates with dates:

```{python}
th = pl.col("time_hour")
{
    "th < pl.datetime(2013, 1, 2, time_zone=NY)": flights_df.filter(
        th < pl.datetime(2013, 1, 2, time_zone="America/New_York")
    ).height,
    "th.dt.date() < date(2013, 1, 2)": flights_df.filter(th.dt.date() < dt.date(2013, 1, 2)).height,
    "th < date(2013, 1, 2)": flights_df.filter(th < dt.date(2013, 1, 2)).height,
}
```

The same rule explains `cast()`: it works on the stored UTC instant, while
`.dt` methods read the local clock. Casting a zoned value to `Date` gives the
UTC date:

```{python}
pl.select(bkk=pl.datetime(2013, 1, 1, 3, time_zone="Asia/Bangkok")).with_columns(
    cast_date=pl.col("bkk").cast(pl.Date),   # UTC: still 31 December
    dt_date=pl.col("bkk").dt.date(),         # local
)
```

**Rule:** change what a `Datetime` means with `.dt` methods
(`replace_time_zone`, `convert_time_zone`, `date`); use `cast()` only to
change the time unit.

### `Date + Duration` drops the hours {#sec-dt-date-plus}

The result is a `Date` whichever side the `Date` is on, so a sub-day
duration is truncated:

```{python}
pl.select(
    plus_5h=pl.date(2013, 1, 1) + pl.duration(hours=5),
    plus_30h=pl.date(2013, 1, 1) + pl.duration(hours=30),
    as_datetime=pl.date(2013, 1, 1).cast(pl.Datetime) + pl.duration(hours=5),
)
```

That is why `make_datetime_100()` starts from `pl.datetime(year, month, day)`,
not `pl.date(...)`. A `Date` plus a bare integer raises; add
`pl.duration(days=n)`.

### Component arithmetic overflows `Int8` {#sec-dt-int8}

Minutes since midnight, the obvious way:

```{python}
pl.select(t=pl.datetime(2013, 1, 1, 23, 59)).with_columns(
    minutes_wrong=pl.col("t").dt.hour() * 60 + pl.col("t").dt.minute(),
    minutes_ok=pl.col("t").dt.hour().cast(pl.Int32) * 60 + pl.col("t").dt.minute(),
)
```

`hour()` is `Int8` and the literal `60` fits in `Int8`, so the product stays
`Int8` and wraps ([Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-overflow)).
Widen first, or avoid the arithmetic:
`(t - t.dt.truncate("1d")).dt.total_minutes()`. The same trap waits in
`month() * 100 + day()`.

## Recipes {#sec-dt-recipes}

**Flights per weekday** (`count(wday = wday(dep_time, label = TRUE))`): group
by the number and the name, sort by the number.

```{python}
flights_df_dt.group_by(
    wday=pl.col("dep_time").dt.weekday(),
    name=pl.col("dep_time").dt.strftime("%a"),
).agg(n=pl.len()).sort("wday")
```

**Average delay by scheduled hour of day:**

```{python}
flights_df_dt.group_by(hour=pl.col("sched_dep_time").dt.hour()).agg(
    avg_delay=pl.col("dep_delay").mean().round(1),
    n=pl.len(),
).sort("hour")
```

**Fix overnight arrivals.** `make_datetime_100()` gave arrivals the departure
date, so a flight landing after midnight seems to arrive before it left.
R4DS adds `days(overnight)`; `pl.duration()` needs a number, so cast the
Boolean:

```{python}
flights_df_fixed = flights_df_dt.with_columns(
    overnight=pl.col("arr_time") < pl.col("dep_time")
).with_columns(
    pl.col("arr_time", "sched_arr_time") + pl.duration(days=pl.col("overnight").cast(pl.Int64))
)

{
    "overnight flights": flights_df_fixed["overnight"].sum(),
    "still arriving before departure": flights_df_fixed.filter(
        pl.col("arr_time") < pl.col("dep_time")
    ).height,
}
```

`arr_time` is local to the destination, so `arr_time - dep_time` is still not
the flight's elapsed time.

**Convert clinic times between zones.** A Bangkok clinic books 21:00
teleconsults with a New York team. The clock gap is 12 hours until New York
switches to DST, then 11:

```{python}
consults_df = pl.DataFrame({"slot": ["2013-03-09 21:00", "2013-03-10 21:00"]}).with_columns(
    bkk=pl.col("slot").str.to_datetime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M", time_zone="Asia/Bangkok"),
).with_columns(
    ny=pl.col("bkk").dt.convert_time_zone("America/New_York"),
).with_columns(
    clock_gap=pl.col("bkk").dt.replace_time_zone(None) - pl.col("ny").dt.replace_time_zone(None),
)
consults_df
```

`clock_gap` compares the two wall clocks: drop both zones, then subtract.
Subtracting the zoned columns directly raises (different dtypes), and once
converted to one zone they are the same instant.
